newsitem.title: UK: Nitric oxide may be key to migraine help - report.
newsitem.headline: Nitric oxide may be key to migraine help - report.

text.p: A chemical that regulates blood pressure and many other bodily functions may hold the key to treating migraines, Danish researchers reported on Friday.
Migraine sufferers given a drug that stops production of the chemical, nitric oxide, said their symptoms improved noticeably, Lisbeth Lassen of Copenhagen's Glostrup Hospital reported.
Lassen's group gave the drug, Glaxo Wellcome's 546C88, to 15 migraine sufferers and sugar water to 14 others.
"They had all come into the centre in an acute migraine attack," Lassen said in a telephone interview.
Within two hours nine of those given the drug said their symptoms eased to a moderate headache, while five of those given placebo did.
"The effect on migraine pain (and sensitivity to sound and light) was significant," Lassen wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.

"Nitric oxide seems to be involved not only in the initiation of migraine attacks as previously suggested, but also in the maintenance of these attacks. Inhibiting NO production or reducing the effects of NO may therefore represent a completely novel therapeutic principle in migraine."
Nitric oxide dilates blood vessels, regulating blood pressure. It also plays a key role in the brain and is involved in septic shock, when the body becomes overwhelmed by infection.
The drug 546C88, still considered experimental, was developed for use against septic shock but Larsen said her findings could open new avenues for using drugs that inhibit nitric oxide.
"This is the first time such a drug has been used in this way," she said. "It is promising."
The drug did, however, raise the blood pressure and slow the heartbeat of the volunteers.

Larsen said it 546C88 worked against all three forms of NO synthase -- an enzyme key to NO production. A better migraine drug would be more specific and target only the type involved in headache, leaving blood pressure and heartbeat alone.
Six percent of men and 14 to 18 percent of women in industrialised countries complain of migraine. The debilitating headaches are often accompanied by nausea and hallucinations.
Dozens of drugs, ranging from aspirin to beta-blockers, are used to treat migraine. None has been found completely effective and many have dangerous side-effects.
